newsitem.title: GERMANY: Minister wants to accelerate Telekom sale.
newsitem.headline: Minister wants to accelerate Telekom sale.

text.p: German Posts and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch said on Tuesday that Bonn would sell off shares in Deutsche Telekom AG faster than planned to help cut borrowing and qualify for European Monetary Union (EMU).
"We will certainly sell our shares faster than had hitherto been planned," Boetsch told German news channel n-TV according to extracts from an interview to be aired later in the day.
Boetsch added that how state-owned shares in the German telephone monopoly would be sold had not yet been decided, but he was looking at three options. They were:
-- A bourse flotation, which would not require legislation,
-- The sale of shares to a strategic partner,
-- The disposal of the state's entire stake.

Referring to Germany's difficulties in qualifying for EMU, Boetsch said the privatisation would take place in such a timely way that "the problems were are now facing can be dealt with satisfactorily".
That meant Finance Minister Theo Waigel should be able to book the proceeds of a further Telekom sale during the current year. "It must be realisable," Boetsch said.
Bonn still controls nearly three-quarters of Telekom after last November's successful privatisation of a 26 percent stake, which raised 20 billion marks.
Boetsch repudiated charges that Bonn was simply raiding its own assets to make the grade for Europe's single currency.
"Nothing is being plundered," he told n-tv. "We are also not selling under pressure. This is not some kind of carpet trading where prices can be dictated."
Asked whether a Japanese partner might buy into Telekom, Boetsch said he was not aware of such interest.
News weekly Der Spiegel reported on Monday that Japanese phone giant Nippon Telegraph & Telephone Corp (NTT) was examining possible acquisitions in Germany, including buying into Deutsche Telekom.
Spiegel also reported that Telekom chief executive Ron Sommer had been courting NTT for some time in a bid to build a strategic alliance covering Asia.
-- Douglas Busvine, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150

The 287 million shares could be parked with a bank and later sold to a strategic partner of Telekom, the sources said. The shares would then be sold on the market by 2000 at the earliest, they said.
That sale could bring Bonn about 11 billion marks at Telekom's current share price.
The coalition needs the money to help close a deficit worsened by an expected nine billion mark shortfall in 1997 tax revenue and near-record unemployment rolls.
Bonn owns 2.03 billion shares in Telekom, the former state-owned phone monopoly. Telekom offered its first tranche of shares to the market in an initial public offering last November.
